ladders.title: Stretch then rotate: F, C, E and the rotation trap
ladders.freq: Newer topic list; finite kinematics underlies the Fall 2025 simple shear and Spring 2025 balloon questions
ladders.figure: A unit square with corner at the origin, axes X₁ and X₂. It is stretched by λ along X₁, then rotated rigidly by θ; the reference square is dashed.

rungs.ask: Write F for this motion.
rungs.answer: F = RU with U = [[λ, 0], [0, 1]] and R = [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]], so F = [[λ cos θ, −sin θ], [λ sin θ, cos θ]] and J = λ.
rungs.say: F equals R times U, stretch first, then rotation

rungs.ask: Compute C.
rungs.answer: C = FᵀF = UᵀRᵀRU = U² = [[λ², 0], [0, 1]]; the rotation cancels because RᵀR = I.
rungs.say: C equals F transpose F, and the rotation cancels

rungs.ask: Green-Lagrange strain?
rungs.answer: E = ½(C − I) = [[½(λ² − 1), 0], [0, 0]], a pure stretch along X₁ whatever θ is.
rungs.say: E is one half of C minus I, and it sees only the stretch

rungs.ask: Now give me the small strain tensor.
rungs.answer: ε = ½(H + Hᵀ) with H = F − I: ε₁₁ = λ cos θ − 1, ε₂₂ = cos θ − 1, ε₁₂ = ½(λ − 1) sin θ.
rungs.say: ε is the symmetric part of the displacement gradient, F minus I

rungs.ask: Set λ = 1. What does each measure say?
rungs.answer: A pure rotation gives E = 0, while ε₁₁ = ε₂₂ = cos θ − 1 ≈ −θ²/2, a spurious compression from a rigid motion.
rungs.say: For a rigid rotation E is zero and ε shows a spurious θ²/2 compression

rungs.ask: So when is ε good enough?
rungs.answer: When the displacement gradient is small: small strains and small rotations, so the θ² error stays well below the strains of interest.
rungs.say: ε works when strains and rotations are both small

rungs.ask: Give the strain of the X₁ fibre in each measure.
rungs.answer: Engineering λ − 1, Green ½(λ² − 1), logarithmic ln λ; all equal λ − 1 to first order, and in tension Green is the largest and logarithmic the smallest.
rungs.say: All three agree to first order in λ minus 1

rungs.ask: Which tensors live in the current configuration?
rungs.answer: B = FFᵀ = R U² Rᵀ and the Almansi strain e = ½(I − B⁻¹) are spatial: they carry the principal directions rotated by θ.
rungs.say: B and the Almansi strain live in the current configuration

ladders.trap: Build strain from C = FᵀF so the rotation cancels, and use ε only when the rotations are small as well as the strains.

ladders.title: Cauchy to Piola on a rotated bar, then objectivity
ladders.freq: On the classic slips list: P = JσF⁻ᵀ and σ* = QσQᵀ
ladders.figure: A bar of length L₀ and area A₀ along e₁ carries axial force N. In the current configuration it is stretched by λ, incompressible, and rotated by θ so its axis is n.

rungs.ask: Cauchy stress in the deformed bar?
rungs.answer: Current area a = A₀/λ since J = 1, so σ = (λN/A₀) n ⊗ n: true force over current area along the current axis.
rungs.say: Cauchy stress is force over current area

rungs.ask: Now the first Piola stress.
rungs.answer: P = JσF⁻ᵀ. With F⁻¹n = e₁/λ this gives P = (N/A₀) n ⊗ e₁: current force over reference area.
rungs.say: P equals J σ F inverse transpose

rungs.ask: Is P symmetric?
rungs.answer: P is a two-point tensor with one leg in each configuration, generally unsymmetric; angular momentum balance makes PFᵀ symmetric.
rungs.say: P is a two-point tensor, and P F transpose is the symmetric one

rungs.ask: Second Piola stress?
rungs.answer: S = F⁻¹P = (N/(λA₀)) e₁ ⊗ e₁, symmetric and entirely in the reference configuration, free of the rotation θ.
rungs.say: S equals F inverse P, fully in the reference configuration

rungs.ask: Superpose a further rigid rotation Q on the loaded bar. How does each stress change?
rungs.answer: F* = QF, so σ* = QσQᵀ, P* = QP and S* = S.
rungs.say: Cauchy rotates on both legs, P on its spatial leg, and S stays put

rungs.ask: What does objectivity demand of a constitutive law?
rungs.answer: σ(QF) = Qσ(F)Qᵀ for every rotation Q; equivalently S depends on F only through C, S = Ŝ(C).
rungs.say: The law must give σ star equal to Q σ Q transpose

rungs.ask: Why use S for the law and σ for strength?
rungs.answer: S is work conjugate to E and unchanged by rotation, so S = ∂W/∂E is natural; σ is the true force per deformed area that yield and fracture criteria use.
rungs.say: S suits the constitutive law and σ suits the strength check

rungs.ask: Small strain limit?
rungs.answer: As F → I with small rotation, J → 1 and σ, P and S coincide to first order.
rungs.say: At small strain all three stresses coincide

ladders.trap: Write P = JσF⁻ᵀ with the inverse transpose, track which leg of each stress lives in which configuration, and under a superposed rotation use σ* = QσQᵀ and S* = S.

ladders.title: Airy from equilibrium to compatibility to a cantilever
ladders.freq: On the classic slips list: the Airy minus sign and the biharmonic from compatibility
ladders.figure: A cantilever of length L, depth 2c and unit thickness, axes x along the span and y up at the free end, clamped at x = L, with a downward tip shear load P at x = 0.

rungs.ask: Write plane equilibrium with zero body force.
rungs.answer: ∂σ₁₁/∂x + ∂σ₁₂/∂y = 0 and ∂σ₁₂/∂x + ∂σ₂₂/∂y = 0.
rungs.say: Two equilibrium equations in the plane

rungs.ask: Define the Airy stress function.
rungs.answer: σ₁₁ = ∂²φ/∂y², σ₂₂ = ∂²φ/∂x², σ₁₂ = −∂²φ/∂x∂y; substituting satisfies both equilibrium equations identically.
rungs.say: With the minus sign on the shear, equilibrium is automatic

rungs.ask: Then where does the biharmonic come from?
rungs.answer: From compatibility ∂²ε₁₁/∂y² + ∂²ε₂₂/∂x² = 2∂²ε₁₂/∂x∂y, written in stresses with Hooke's law, giving ∇⁴φ = 0.
rungs.say: The biharmonic comes from compatibility

rungs.ask: Does it depend on plane stress or plane strain?
rungs.answer: With zero body force ∇⁴φ = 0 in both; the elastic constants drop out, so the stresses are the same.
rungs.say: With zero body force the biharmonic holds in both

rungs.ask: Pick φ for the cantilever.
rungs.answer: φ = A xy + B xy³: σ₁₁ = 6Bxy, σ₂₂ = 0, σ₁₂ = −A − 3By², and ∇⁴φ = 0.
rungs.say: Bending moment grows with x, so I need x y cubed

rungs.ask: Apply the conditions on y = ±c.
rungs.answer: σ₂₂ = 0 already; σ₁₂(±c) = 0 gives A = −3Bc², so σ₁₂ = 3B(c² − y²).
rungs.say: Traction free faces fix A in terms of B

rungs.ask: And at the loaded end x = 0?
rungs.answer: Outward normal −x gives traction t_y = −σ₁₂; summing to the downward load −P gives ∫σ₁₂ dy = P, so 4Bc³ = P and B = P/(6I) with I = 2c³/3.
rungs.say: I match the shear resultant to P in the Saint-Venant sense

rungs.ask: Final stresses, and check them.
rungs.answer: σ₁₁ = Pxy/I, σ₂₂ = 0, σ₁₂ = (P/(2I))(c² − y²): flexure formula with M = Px, tension on top as a hogging cantilever needs, and peak shear 3P/(2A) at the neutral axis with A = 2c.
rungs.say: This is the flexure formula plus parabolic shear

rungs.ask: How good is it at the clamp?
rungs.answer: Exact only for end tractions with this linear and parabolic shape; a real clamp differs locally, and by Saint-Venant the solution holds about a beam depth away from it.
rungs.say: Saint-Venant makes it accurate a depth away from the clamp

ladders.trap: Define σ₁₂ = −∂²φ/∂x∂y with the minus sign so equilibrium is automatic, get ∇⁴φ = 0 from compatibility, and fix the constants with the face conditions and the end resultant.

ladders.title: Lamé cylinder to the 1/r³ sphere to a shrink fit
ladders.freq: On the classic slips list: the sphere uses 1/r³ Lamé and its bore state is equibiaxial plus radial
ladders.figure: Three sketches: a thick cylinder with inner radius a, outer radius b and internal pressure p; a thick sphere with the same a, b, p; a ring shrunk onto a solid shaft with radial interference δ.

rungs.ask: Thick cylinder: set it up.
rungs.answer: Equilibrium dσ_rr/dr + (σ_rr − σ_θθ)/r = 0 with ε_rr = du/dr and ε_θθ = u/r gives u = C₁r + C₂/r.
rungs.say: Axisymmetric equilibrium plus Hooke's law gives u equals C₁ r plus C₂ over r

rungs.ask: Stresses?
rungs.answer: σ_rr = A − B/r², σ_θθ = A + B/r²; σ_rr(a) = −p and σ_rr(b) = 0 give A = pa²/(b² − a²), B = pa²b²/(b² − a²).
rungs.say: The Lamé form is A minus B over r squared

rungs.ask: Where is the peak, and check the thin limit.
rungs.answer: Peak hoop stress at the bore, σ_θθ(a) = p(b² + a²)/(b² − a²); with b = a + t and t ≪ a this tends to pa/t.
rungs.say: The bore carries the peak and the thin limit gives p a over t

rungs.ask: Now a thick sphere. What changes?
rungs.answer: Two equal hoop directions give dσ_rr/dr + 2(σ_rr − σ_θθ)/r = 0, u = C₁r + C₂/r², so σ_rr = C − 2D/r³ and σ_θθ = σ_φφ = C + D/r³.
rungs.say: The sphere has a factor 2 in equilibrium and goes as 1 over r cubed

rungs.ask: Apply the boundary conditions.
rungs.answer: C = pa³/(b³ − a³), D = pa³b³/(2(b³ − a³)); bore hoop stress p(2a³ + b³)/(2(b³ − a³)), and the thin limit gives pa/(2t).
rungs.say: Same boundary conditions, and the thin limit gives p a over 2 t

rungs.ask: Why can Airy give you the cylinder but the sphere needs this route?
rungs.answer: Airy is a plane construct and the cylinder is a plane problem; the sphere is fully three dimensional with an equibiaxial hoop state plus radial compression at the bore.
rungs.say: Airy is a plane construct, so the sphere comes from 3D equilibrium

rungs.ask: Shrink a ring a to b onto a solid shaft of radius a, same material. Interface pressure?
rungs.answer: Interference equals ring bore growth plus shaft shrinkage: δ = (pa/E)((b² + a²)/(b² − a²) + ν) + (pa/E)(1 − ν), so p = Eδ(b² − a²)/(2ab²) in plane stress.
rungs.say: The interference equals the ring growth plus the shaft shrinkage

rungs.ask: Where does the assembly yield first?
rungs.answer: At the ring bore: σ_θθ = p(b² + a²)/(b² − a²) and σ_rr = −p, so Tresca gives σ_θθ − σ_rr = 2pb²/(b² − a²); the shaft sits in uniform compression −p.
rungs.say: The ring bore yields first

ladders.trap: Write sphere equilibrium with the factor 2 on (σ_rr − σ_θθ)/r so the solution carries 1/r³, and set the shrink fit interference equal to the ring bore growth plus the shaft shrinkage.

ladders.title: Fibre stiffness bounds to a lamina to cure stresses
ladders.freq: Asked Spring 2026 as a particle composite; the series estimate as the lower (Reuss) bound is on the classic slips list
ladders.figure: Two blocks of alternating fibre and matrix layers, one loaded along the layers and one across them; a unidirectional lamina with axes 1 along the fibres and 2 across; a [0/90] two-ply cooled from cure.

rungs.ask: Fibre E_f, matrix E_m, fibre fraction V_f. Stiffness along the layers?
rungs.answer: Equal strain in both phases (iso-strain, parallel): E₁ = V_f E_f + (1 − V_f) E_m, the Voigt estimate.
rungs.say: Along the fibres both phases share the strain, so the moduli add

rungs.ask: Across the layers?
rungs.answer: Equal stress (iso-stress, series): 1/E₂ = V_f/E_f + (1 − V_f)/E_m, the Reuss estimate.
rungs.say: Across the layers both phases share the stress, so the compliances add

rungs.ask: Which one bounds what?
rungs.answer: For phases with equal Poisson ratios, Voigt is the upper bound and Reuss the lower bound on the effective modulus of any arrangement, from minimum potential and minimum complementary energy; Reuss holds as a lower bound for any Poisson ratios, and the true transverse modulus of a fibre lamina sits above Reuss.
rungs.say: Voigt is the upper bound and Reuss the lower bound

rungs.ask: Sketch both against V_f.
rungs.answer: Voigt is a straight line from E_m to E_f; Reuss sags and stays near E_m until V_f is high; the gap widens as E_f/E_m grows.
rungs.say: Voigt is linear and Reuss hugs the matrix modulus

rungs.ask: What constants describe the lamina in plane stress?
rungs.answer: Four: E₁, E₂, ν₁₂, G₁₂, with reciprocity ν₂₁ = ν₁₂E₂/E₁; the lamina is transversely isotropic about the fibre.
rungs.say: Four in-plane constants: E₁, E₂, ν₁₂ and G₁₂

rungs.ask: Write the lamina stiffness matrix.
rungs.answer: Q₁₁ = E₁/(1 − ν₁₂ν₂₁), Q₂₂ = E₂/(1 − ν₁₂ν₂₁), Q₁₂ = ν₁₂E₂/(1 − ν₁₂ν₂₁), Q₆₆ = G₁₂; rotate it to Q̄ for an off-axis ply.
rungs.say: Q comes from inverting the plane stress compliance

rungs.ask: Cool a free lamina from cure. What happens inside it?
rungs.answer: It shrinks freely by α₁ΔT and α₂ΔT, α₁ small and α₂ large; inside, the matrix wants to shrink more than the fibres, so the matrix carries axial tension and the fibres axial compression, self-equilibrated.
rungs.say: The free lamina is stress free overall and the phases carry self-equilibrated residual stress

rungs.ask: Bond a 0° ply to a 90° ply and cool.
rungs.answer: Along x the 90° ply contracts by α₂ΔT and the 0° ply by α₁ΔT, so the 90° ply goes into transverse tension and the 0° ply into compression; the unsymmetric [0/90] has B ≠ 0 and warps, while [0/90]s stays flat and keeps the residual stresses.
rungs.say: The ply that wants to shrink more ends up in tension

rungs.ask: Why does that matter?
rungs.answer: Transverse tension in the 90° plies adds to service load and drives transverse matrix cracking, the first ply failure in cross-ply laminates.
rungs.say: Cure stress uses up transverse strength in the 90 degree plies

ladders.trap: Name the iso-strain (Voigt) and iso-stress (Reuss) assumptions, place them as the upper and lower bounds, and after cure put the ply with the larger contraction into tension.
